Same failure here, reproduced from a Letta Code 0.28.17 client on Windows 11, routed through the opencode-go / Console Go provider. Two separate request paths hit it:

1. Inline parent model: openai Chat Completions API stream failed (400): Error from provider (Console Go): Upstream request failed (run run-72d04346-1209-40b2-b32f-e4b10fa70bec).
2. Background subagent call — classified llm_bad_request / invalid_request_error, retryable: false (subagent subagent-1785271150477-6, task task_6).

The Letta server constructs the request payload server-side, so I don't have the exact sampling-parameter values from the failing call. I checked local config (%USERPROFILE%\.letta\*.json, including the bundled model catalog) and recent *.log files — none of them contain the request body, so I can't confirm whether top_p=0, temperature=0, reasoning_effort, or thinking is the trigger. Reporting those as the cause from my side would be speculation.

What I can say is that the failure is reproducible from a third-party client (Letta Code) talking to Console Go, and the error is surfaced verbatim — so the 400 is being returned by Console Go / opencode.ai, not invented by the client. This corroborates the umbrella pattern in #37056 and overlaps with the parameter-related report in #37231 (where the underlying Invalid top_p value, the valid range of top_p is (0, 1.0] message was exposed and setting top_p/temperature to null restored functionality).

Environment: Letta Code 0.28.17, Windows 11, parent model chatgpt-plus-pro/gpt-5.6-terra with reasoning_effort=medium, max_output_tokens=128000, context window 350000.

Happy to enable debug-level provider logging on the Letta side if that helps isolate the parameter set that Console Go is rejecting.

+1 to keeping #37056 as the umbrella for this family rather than opening a new report.

I implemented this same feature independently before I found your PR — yours is further along (docs, config schema, SDK types), so I'm standing down and would rather help this one land. Four things from digging through the earlier attempt in #8359 that I think are the actual blockers worth pre-empting:

1. **The new config options.** @rekram1-node's notes there start with "ideally no extra config option" ([comment](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/8359#issuecomment-3747840409)), and that author dropped theirs in response — "1. No extra config option" ([comment](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/8359#issuecomment-3752576435)). This PR adds `enable_model_discovery` and `disable_model_discovery`, so it will probably hit the same objection. Your code comment has a fair rationale (it's an outbound request to a user-supplied URL) — might be worth making that argument up front, or keying off "provider is config-declared/authed" rather than a new flag.

2. **Union vs. filter.** The same note asks discovery to *remove* models too: if models.dev lists N and the endpoint returns N-2, the missing 2 should be dropped as unsupported. Right now discovery only adds ids that aren't already known, so stale models.dev entries stick around. (My version had this same gap.)

3. **Timeout.** `AbortSignal.timeout(5_000)` vs. the "1-3 sec tops" ask in that review. This runs on the provider-load path, so an unreachable endpoint adds the full delay to startup.

4. Minor: discovered models that models.dev doesn't know get `limit.context: 0` / `limit.output: 0` via `buildConfigModel(..., {}, ...)`. That's fine for config-declared models where the user omitted limits, but with discovery it becomes the common case — probably worth confirming nothing downstream (compaction/context math) depends on a real context limit.

Reusing `buildConfigModel` for discovered models is nicer than what I did (I hand-rolled a minimal `Model`) — this way anything models.dev already knows keeps its real metadata and variants.

Taking this one if nobody's on it. The `K` branch formats `num / 1000` with `toFixed(1)`, so anything from 999,950 up rounds to `1000.0K` before the `>= 1000000` check can promote it to `M`. Fix is to roll over at 999,950 — the point where one-decimal rounding reaches 1000.0K — so those values format as `1.0M`. Sending a PR with a unit test shortly.

Still present in **1.18.9**, five releases on from the 1.17.8 report here. Adding forensics that I think pin the mechanism down further, plus a recovery trap that I suspect is sending people to the wrong conclusion.

**It took the whole machine down, not just the TUI.** CPU pegged at 99%+ and stayed there; the box needed a hard restart, which took unrelated services with it.

**Forensic signature.** I had four preserved snapshot dirs under `~/.local/share/opencode/snapshot/`. Exactly one had a stale `index.lock` — and it was the only one whose git config read `worktree = <my home dir>`. The other three, all scoped to ordinary project dirs, were clean:

| snapshot worktree | stale index.lock |
|---|---|
| `<home dir>` | yes |
| `<home>/src/<project>` | no |
| `<home>/src/<project2>` | no |
| `/tmp/<scratch>/<repo>` | no |

In the failing one: `index` written at 13:35:30 (145 bytes, essentially empty), `index.lock` taken at 13:38:28 and never released, `refs/` empty and `packed-refs` holding no refs — so no snapshot ever completed, it just churned. Config carried `manyFiles = true`, `untrackedCache = true`, `index.version = 4`.

Scale of that root: **395,448** files git considers, with a 0-byte `.gitignore`, so `node_modules`, caches, editor server dirs and backups were all in scope.

**Counter-test.** The same 1.18.9 binary scoped to a small throwaway repo with `--dir` returned in a few seconds, load stayed ~1.0, CPU never registered, snapshot written correctly. So it is specific to the size/shape of the project root, exactly as described above.

**The recovery trap — this is the part I would most like to see addressed.** After the hard restart the process re-spun on launch. That reads exactly like corrupt-database recovery, so the natural response is to discard the database. We did. It does not help, because the trigger is the project root, not the database. We only found the real cause by going through the snapshot dirs by hand. Anyone without that instinct would conclude their db was corrupt and lose it for nothing.

**Why I think this deserves more than a config-flag workaround.** The project root is just wherever the process was started, so forgetting which directory you are in is enough to trigger it, with no prompt and no indication that hundreds of thousands of files are about to be indexed. In my experience other agentic CLI tools in this category run from a home directory without incident — I keep working notes in mine for exactly that reason, since it is where the tool already is. That habit is harmless everywhere else I have used it and machine-fatal here, which makes it a migration hazard rather than a misconfiguration.

Suggestions, roughly in order of how much they would have helped me:

- Clean up or surface a stale `index.lock` on start rather than re-spinning on it — this alone would have prevented the wrong diagnosis.
- Cap or short-circuit above a file-count threshold, with a clear log line naming the root being indexed.
- Warn, or require opt-in, when the project root is `$HOME`.
- Make snapshot progress visible so a hang is diagnosable without going through the snapshot dirs manually.

Happy to supply more detail from the preserved snapshot dirs if it is useful.

Two interim workarounds, for anyone landing here before this is fixed. Neither needs `snapshot: false`, so you keep undo/revert.

**1. Shrink what the snapshot has to index.** The snapshot walks what git considers, so a real `.gitignore` at the project root fixes it directly. My home directory had a 0-byte one; filling it in took the tree from **395,458 files to 357** — dot-directories alone were 69% of it:

```gitignore
/.*
!/.gitignore
/miniconda3/
/go/
/snap/
/backups/
```

After that a snapshot from the same root is instant. Nothing gets un-tracked by this — ignoring only affects untracked files.

**2. Refuse the launch outright.** The real failure mode is forgetting which directory you are in, so the durable fix is to make that impossible rather than remember every time:

```bash
opencode() {
  if [ "$PWD" = "$HOME" ]; then
    echo "refusing: opencode from \$HOME — use 'opencode --dir <project>'" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  command opencode "$@"
}
```

Note this only applies to interactive shells, since `.bashrc` typically returns early when non-interactive — scripts or agents spawning `opencode` will bypass it. A wrapper earlier in `PATH` covers that case if you need it.

**One diagnostic detail that might be useful to whoever picks this up:** I tested `opencode run --dir` against a directory that was *not* a git repo, and no snapshot directory was created at all — the snapshot path only engages when the project root is already a git repo. So the trigger is specifically "project root is a git repo containing a very large working tree", which may narrow down where a size guard belongs.

Adding a related perspective from the operator side.

I'd like to configure webfetch to honestly identify as an AI agent (e.g. something like `opencode-ai/1.18.7 (+https://opencode.ai)`) instead of impersonating Chrome. Currently there is no way to do this — the User-Agent is hardcoded in `packages/opencode/src/tool/webfetch.ts`:

```ts
const headers = {
  "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/143.0.0.0 Safari/537.36",
  ...
}
```

The only fallback path uses `User-Agent: opencode`, which (as #33074 points out) is even worse than nothing.

Two reasons I'd argue for making this configurable:

1. **Server-side ethics**: impersonating a browser misleads site operators about the nature of the traffic hitting their logs. Several jurisdictions (e.g. EU AI Act disclosure requirements, plus the general principle of honest user-agents per RFC 9110 §10.1.5) lean toward agents disclosing themselves.
2. **Lower friction with bot-detection systems like Anubis**, which is exactly the case you raised — honesty is rewarded.

A minimal change would be:

- Add an optional `user_agent` parameter (or a top-level `webfetch.user_agent` config setting) that overrides the default.
- If unset, keep the current Chrome spoof as the default for backward compatibility.

This would unblock both transparency-conscious operators and users hitting Anubis/Cloudflare honestly, without forcing a breaking change on anyone who relies on the current default.

Additional macOS production evidence from 2026-07-28: `~/.local/share/opencode/tool-output` reached 33 GiB with 6,600+ spill entries. No owning cleanup command surfaced; deleting the spill files manually reduced the OpenCode store from 97 GiB to 65 GiB. The files were independent of the 64 GiB SQLite database. Please include startup/periodic orphan reconciliation, active-session protection, aggregate byte limits, and a user-facing `opencode storage cleanup --dry-run/--apply` path in acceptance.

Case for native: it works with no config on a default install, `deny` rules and existing `always` grants keep working, and subagent sessions are never auto-approved since a subagent's prompt is model written. In a plugin the permissions evaluation will be outside core.

Taking this if nobody's on it. Confirmed on `dev`: `retryable()` only bypasses the SDK's `isRetryable` flag for `status >= 500`, so a 408 that the SDK didn't mark retryable falls through and ends the turn.

408 Request Timeout is the one 4xx that's transient in the same way 5xx is — the request never completed, so resending it is the defined behavior. Planning to treat it exactly like the existing 5xx case (same code path, same retry/backoff semantics) rather than adding separate handling. PR with tests shortly.

Cross-linking: I filed #39431 for the underlying validation gap that makes this class of bug silent.

Verified on **1.18.9**, the inconsistency is one level of nesting:

- unknown key at config **root** → `Error: Configuration is invalid ... ↳ Unrecognized key: <name>`
- same unknown key nested inside **`mcp.<name>`** → silently discarded, no error, no warning, server reports healthy

So `env` (vs `environment`) is stripped with no diagnostic. @Gelly52 your read that "the config loader silently drops unknown keys instead of erroring" is exactly right, and @hazlamahedich the opaque `-32000 Connection closed` is the downstream symptom of that.

Worth noting the docs half is now fixed — the bundled `customize-opencode` skill says `environment` in 1.18.9 (it said `env` in 1.18.5, per #39135). But the silent-drop behavior is unchanged, so configs written against the older skill keep failing silently after upgrade. Homebrew is also still shipping 1.18.5, so new `brew` users still get the skill that teaches the stripped key.

In my case this silently loaded a different `dbt-mcp` toolset than configured — every `DISABLE_*` flag ignored, and write tools exposed despite being explicitly disabled, while the server reported healthy. Details in #39431.
